cases.why: Zero, the baseline.
Sub-cent: real spend stays visible rather than rounding away to a misleading $0.00.
Sub-cent, nearer the floor than the case above.
An exact half rounds AWAY FROM ZERO, so this is a real figure rather than '< $0.01'.
One cent — the floor as a figure.

The classic half. As a double this is 0.014999..., yet both sides must round it UP, because Intl rounds the number's shortest decimal representation and str() of a float is that same representation. Fails if the backend reaches for Decimal(value) instead of Decimal(str(value)), or if the frontend is 'simplified' from toLocaleString to toFixed, which uses the binary value.
Same trap as 0.015, one unit up.
Same trap again; page said $2.68 and a truncating PDF said $2.67.
THE REPORTED BUG: the page said $0.06 and the PDF said $0.05.
A value whose double sits a hair BELOW the cent; truncation printed $0.28. Ordinary, not an edge case.
Same again.
Same again.
Rounds up across the dollar boundary.
Ordinary value.
Ordinary value.
Thousands separator.
Two separators, and rounding at the cent.
The sign goes outside the symbol.
A negative that rounds to nothing loses the sign entirely: '-$0.00' is not a figure.

USD 5.32 and ZAR 2,900 are the two figures this whole change exists for. An ISO code with no symbol in this locale still gets the locale's currency spacing (U+00A0): a CLDR library that skips currencySpacing prints 'ZAR2,900.00' here.
Second multi-currency pair. Same spacing rule.
ZAR DOES have a symbol in en-ZA (and it is 'R', not 'ZAR'), which is why the symbol decision is per (locale, currency) and not per currency.
ICU disambiguates USD to 'US$' in a rand locale, and en-ZA groups with U+00A0 while using ',' as the decimal separator.
Zero-decimal currency in a locale whose group separator is U+00A0: 'JP¥12\u00a0001', not 'JP¥12,001'.
German number shapes with an American currency: the symbol TRAILS, and the group separator is '.'.
The same locale's own currency.
A code with no symbol in German trails the number as well — placement follows the READER, not the currency.
The tiny-spend floor below one yen in a German locale. '< 0.01 €' would be the wrong floor AND the wrong shape.
French group separator is U+202F (narrow no-break space) — not the U+00A0 en-ZA uses — and USD disambiguates to '$US'.
fr-CH writes decimals with '.' and groups with U+202F, unlike fr-FR on both counts.
Swiss German: ASCII apostrophe grouping (CLDR moved this from U+2019), and the symbol LEADS here while de-DE trails it.
de-CH puts the minus AFTER the currency symbol. A formatter that assumes '-' goes before the whole thing gets this wrong.
Four digits are NOT grouped: CLDR's minimumGroupingDigits for it/es/pt/pl/hu is 2, so grouping starts at five digits.
The minimumGroupingDigits case. ICU applies it to the currency pattern but NOT to the plain decimal pattern, so 'format a price the way I format a number' is wrong here.
...and here is where the same locale DOES group.
Same rule, and the code fallback renders as bare 'EUR' rather than a symbol.
Same rule, U+00A0 grouping.
Same rule. Also the locale CLDR itself resolves to the language without a region.
Same rule, with the disambiguated 'US$'.
Same rule, Cyrillic locale, Latin currency code.
Same rule, U+00A0 grouping.
Groups at four digits — the opposite outcome from it-IT, in the same currency.
Finnish uses U+2212 MINUS SIGN, not the ASCII hyphen. Two documents that disagree here are visibly different.
Zero-decimal currency, half rounds up.
ja-JP renders the yen as the FULL-WIDTH U+FFE5, where en-US renders U+00A5.
The tiny floor follows that same full-width glyph: '< \uFFE51'.
A foreign currency in Japanese number shapes.
Chinese yuan: U+00A5 half-width here, and two decimals.
Thai baht.
The rupee symbol, and Latin (not Devanagari) digits.
LAKH GROUPING: the rightmost group is 3 and every group above it is 2 — '12,34,567'. A formatter that only knows groups of three cannot produce this.
Bengali digit shapes AND lakh grouping: '\u09E7\u09E8,\u09E9\u09EA,\u09EB\u09EC\u09ED.\u09EE\u09EF US$'. Reachable only because the digit glyphs are data.
Arabic-Indic digits, Arabic decimal and group separators, a leading RTL mark (U+200F), and the trailing 'US$'. Every one of those is in the table; none of it is arithmetic.
The negative form adds U+061C and U+200E around the minus. A hand-written formatter would have to know ICU's bidi insertion rules to reproduce this.
'R$ 1.234,50' — symbol with a space inside it, '.' grouping, ',' decimals.
THREE fraction digits. A formatter hard-coded to cents cannot print this currency at all.
A well-formed code ICU has no data for: it renders the bare code with the locale's currency spacing, which is the fallback every unlisted currency takes.
The tiny floor is the currency's minor unit, not a literal cent: '< \u00A51'.
